newsitem.title: USA: NYC residents want clothing sales tax ended - poll.
newsitem.headline: NYC residents want clothing sales tax ended - poll.

text.p: By a 90 to 7 margin, New York city residents, who got a taste of what it would be like to pay no clothing sales taxes during a one-week trial in January, want the levy eliminated, a survey found.

New Jersey now gets some of the benefit of the city's comparitively high sales taxes, as 35 percent of the New Yorkers polled by Quinnipiac College said they had bought clothing in the Garden State during the past 12 months. Staten Islanders were the most likely to shop in New Jersey.

Though economists have said that the moratorium on sales taxes from Jan 18 to 24 was too brief from which to draw conclusions, 35 percent of the New Yorkers surveyed told the Hamden, Conn., college that they had splurged by buying more clothes than usual.
About 45 percent said they bought about the same amount of clothes, while nine percent purchased fewer items.

New York City Mayor Rudloph Giuliani, a Republican, and Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan, both want to phase out the state's four percent sales tax on clothing that costs less than $500, along with the city's own four percent levy and a 0.25 percent tax for Metropolitan Transportation Authority.
The Giuliani Administration, which says the city's high sales taxes also drive shoppers to Connecticut, would need permission from Albany to end the levy.

However, Gov George Pataki, a Republican, who proposed his own ambitious package of tax cuts that includes school tax relief and estate and gift tax reductions, has said that while he supports ending the sales tax, it would be hard to do that in the 1998 budget.
Maurice Carroll, the polling institute's director, said New Yorkers believe ending the sales taxes would boost the city's economy.

"New Yorkers offer a rationale for their antipathy to the sales tax on clothes: 64 percent say eliminating the sales tax would help the city's economy, while four percent say it would hurt and 30 percent say it wouldn't make any difference," he said in prepared remarks.
